Hello!

I’ve written an article on how formal verification and AI are reshaping mathematical research.

The motivation: as AI systems become more capable at generating mathematical content, ensuring correctness becomes increasingly important. Formal verification offers a way to provide strong guarantees, and the interaction between both areas opens interesting directions.

The article explores how these approaches complement each other, and what this could mean for the future of mathematical practice.

Article: https://predictablemachines.com/blog/formal-verification-and-ai-are-reshaping-mathematical-research/

Feedback is very welcome!

In the dependent type section , what does this mean

In particular, what dependent types enable that non-dependent types cannot is first-order logic, which is needed to encode most meaningful theorems.

I believe this may be very incorrect , and in general you make the assertion dependent types are what allow us to write math but this is not entirely true either.
Take a look at this to see the relationships between what dependent types give : Lambda cube

I don't think it's incorrect (and it is common) to characterize dependent types as the direction in the lambda cube that enables first-order logic when thinking about it in terms of the Curry-Howard correspondence. Even the lambda cube Wikipedia page you shared mentions this in the λΠ calculus section.

David Mazarro said:

Dependent types do give / can be used to define the LF , but it is not correct to say that’s what dependent types give that non-dependent types do not. FOL is also commonly done without dependent types. Keep in mind I also asked for clarification what this is meant to mean but as read I don’t believe it is correct.
